title: IS CHRISTIANITY ABOUT FOLLOWING RULES?
paragraphs:
IS CHRISTIANITY ABOUT FOLLOWING RULES?
If Christianity is just “be good, obey the rules, and try harder,” then why did Jesus have to die?
There is a version of Christianity that can make you exhausted without ever making you free.
Do this.
Don’t do that.
Read more.
Pray harder.
Stop failing.
Be better.
Try again.
And somewhere between another promise to God and another private failure, you begin wondering whether Christianity is really just an impossible list of rules with Jesus’ name written across the top.
You love God.
Or at least you want to.
But there are things about yourself you don’t want anybody to see.
The thoughts.
The habits.
The anger.
The secret compromises.
The nights when temptation won.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The Bible collecting dust while your phone gets hours of your attention.
The guilt you carry into church beneath clean clothes and a practiced smile.
And perhaps the most painful part is that you already know many of the rules.
Knowing them did not save you.
That is exactly where we need to understand Christianity correctly.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that bad people can save themselves by becoming better rule-followers.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners who could never rescue themselves have been pursued by a holy God through Jesus Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
The Bible does contain commands. Many of them.
Jesus did not abolish holiness. He did not turn obedience into something optional. He never preached a sentimental gospel where sin no longer mattered.
Jesus said:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.”
— John 14:15
So Christianity is certainly not anti-obedience.
But notice the order.
“If you love me…”
Then obedience.
That is radically different from saying, “Obey enough so that maybe I will love you.”
One produces desperate religious performance.
The other produces obedience flowing from relationship with Christ.
And perhaps this is where some of us have misunderstood God for years.
We have been trying to use obedience as currency.
We think:
Maybe if I pray enough, God will accept me.
Maybe if I stop this sin, He will finally want me.
Maybe if I attend church consistently, give money, serve people, read Scripture, clean myself up, and become respectable enough, I can finally stand before Him without shame.
But the Gospel destroys that entire system of spiritual bargaining.
Paul writes:
— Ephesians 2:8–9
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Favor given, not wages earned.
And that matters because Christianity begins with something human pride hates admitting:
You cannot save yourself.
Not because obedience is bad.
Because your problem runs deeper than behavior.
Scripture calls it sin.
The biblical picture is not merely that humanity occasionally breaks some divine regulations. Sin alienates us from God and leaves us unable to manufacture our own righteousness before Him.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23
All.
The respectable religious person.
The addict.
The pastor.
The prisoner.
The woman carrying a secret she has never told anyone.
The man everybody thinks has his life together.
The teenager hiding behind humor.
The church member who knows every worship song but has quietly become cold toward Christ.
You.
Me.
All.
And if Christianity were merely about following rules, the Gospel would not be good news.
It would be a scoreboard.
And every one of us would eventually discover that we lost.
This is why one of the most haunting Hebrew words in Scripture matters.
תּוֹרָה — Torah.
It is commonly translated “law,” but its semantic range includes instruction or teaching. God’s law reveals His holy character and teaches His people how they are to live.
The problem was never that God’s commands were evil.
Paul says plainly:
“So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.”
— Romans 7:12
The problem is us.
A mirror can reveal dirt on your face.
It cannot wash your face.
In a similar way, God’s righteous standard exposes what sin has done to us, but the law is not a ladder by which sinners climb into justification.
Paul writes:
— Romans 3:20
Read that again.
The law exposes.
Jesus saves.
And suddenly the cross begins making sense.
If human beings could become righteous before God simply by trying harder, Calvary would be unnecessary.
If morality could save us, Jesus would not have needed nails.
If religious achievement could reconcile sinners to God, there would have been no reason for the Son of God to bear the cross.
But Christianity does not point to a ladder reaching from earth to heaven.
It points to Christ coming down for us.
John’s Gospel says:
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
— John 1:14
God did not shout instructions from a safe distance.
The eternal Son entered human history.
Jesus touched lepers.
He ate with people society despised.
He confronted hypocritical religion.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He wept.
He suffered.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He was crucified.
And He rose again.
This is not the story of humanity successfully reaching God through religious performance.
It is the story of God acting to redeem sinners through His Son.
And there is a scene in Jesus’ ministry that makes this almost painfully clear.
A Pharisee named Simon invited Jesus to eat with him.
Then a woman entered.
Luke describes her simply as “a woman of the city, who was a sinner.”
She knew what people thought of her.
Imagine walking into a room where your reputation arrives before you do.
Imagine every eye knowing something about your past.
Imagine whispers that do not even need words.
She came to Jesus carrying an alabaster flask of ointment.
Then she stood behind Him weeping.
Her tears fell onto His feet.
She wiped them with her hair.
She kissed His feet.
She anointed them.
And Simon watched.
But he did not see repentance.
He saw scandal.
He thought:
“If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him…”
— Luke 7:39
There it is.
Religion looking at a broken person and seeing only a category.
Sinner.
Dirty.
Unworthy.
Disqualified.
But Jesus knew exactly who was touching Him.
That was the point.
She was not exposing information Jesus did not know.
She was bringing her brokenness to Someone who already knew.
Jesus told Simon a story about two debtors whose debts were canceled, then exposed the difference between Simon’s cold reception and the woman’s overflowing response.
And then Jesus said words she may have desperately needed to hear:
“Your sins are forgiven.”
— Luke 7:48
Not hidden.
Forgiven.
Not excused.
Forgiven.
Not renamed.
Forgiven.
That is grace.
Grace does not look at evil and call it good.
Grace looks at guilty people who come to Christ and offers what they could never purchase for themselves.
Forgiveness.
This is why the Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated “repentance,” matters so much.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It involves a genuine turning—a changed mind and orientation toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our self-esteem while leaving us enslaved to the very sins destroying us.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Mark records Jesus proclaiming:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.”
— Mark 1:15
Grace is free.
Grace is not cheap.
There is a difference.
You cannot purchase salvation.
Christ purchased redemption at a cost we could never pay.
Peter writes that believers were ransomed not with silver or gold,
“but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.”
— 1 Peter 1:19
So what happens to obedience?
It finally gets put in its proper place.
We do not obey Christ in order to force Him to save us.
Those who belong to Christ are called to obey because He has saved them, because they love Him, because His Spirit is at work in them, because grace does not merely pardon—it transforms.
That is why stopping at Ephesians 2:9 gives an incomplete picture.
Immediately after saying salvation is not the result of works, Paul continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.”
— Ephesians 2:10
Do you see it?
Not saved by good works.
Saved for good works.
Works are not the root of our salvation.
They become fruit.
Jesus gives a similar picture:
“I am the vine; you are the branches.”
— John 15:5
A branch does not grit its teeth and manufacture life.
It abides.
Life flows from the vine.
Then fruit appears.
This is why Christianity without transformation is also a distortion of the Gospel.
Grace is not permission to make peace with sin.
Paul anticipated exactly that misunderstanding:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!”
— Romans 6:1–2
The Gospel rescues us from two cliffs.
On one side is legalism:
“I obey, therefore God must accept me.”
On the other is lawlessness:
“God accepts me, therefore obedience does not matter.”
The Gospel says something far more beautiful:
In Christ, salvation is God’s gift received through faith, and the grace that forgives begins transforming the person who has been forgiven.
You are not being invited merely to become religious.
You are being called to Christ.
And maybe this is where the article stops being theology on a screen and becomes painfully personal.
Because some people reading this have been performing Christianity.
You know how to look saved.
You know when to say amen.
You know the songs.
You know the vocabulary.
You know which sins Christians condemn publicly.
But you also know what happens when nobody is watching.
Maybe you have spent years polishing the outside while something inside you has been dying.
Jesus spoke directly to religious leaders who mastered appearances while neglecting inward reality.
He said:
“For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence.”
— Matthew 23:25
That warning should frighten every person who knows how to perform religion.
Because Jesus is not looking for a better costume.
He wants the heart.
And somebody reading this may have the opposite problem.
You are not pretending to be righteous.
You feel too ruined to come home.
You think your scandal is bigger than His grace.
You have crossed lines.
Broken vows.
Hurt people.
Returned to sins you swore you would never touch again.
Maybe you have whispered:
“God must be finished with me.”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin is insignificant.
It tells you that Christ is a greater Savior than you imagined.
Paul wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners…”
— 1 Timothy 1:15
Jesus did not come looking for people who could prove they never needed saving.
He came to save sinners.
That does not mean everybody is automatically reconciled to God regardless of their response to Christ.
The New Testament repeatedly calls people to repentance and faith.
But it means your past does not possess greater saving power than Jesus possesses redeeming power.
Look at Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then denied Jesus three times.
Imagine hearing the rooster.
Imagine remembering Christ’s prediction.
Imagine realizing that, at the moment courage mattered, you failed.
Luke says Peter “went out and wept bitterly.”
But Peter’s failure did not become the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
“Do you love me?”
Jesus asked.
And then:
“Feed my sheep.”
See the movement.
Failure.
Grief.
Restoration.
Calling.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending Peter never denied Him.
Jesus rewrote Peter’s story by meeting the fallen disciple with restoring grace and calling him forward in faithful obedience.
That distinction matters.
Jesus does not redeem our stories by editing sin out of history.
He redeems us by refusing to let sin have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is Christianity.
Not “follow enough rules and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
Not “do whatever you want because grace means nothing matters.”
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Grace that forgives.
Truth that exposes.
Repentance that turns.
Faith that receives.
The Holy Spirit transforming.
A new life learning obedience from love.
And maybe now you understand why you have been so tired.
You have been trying to carry a Christianity Jesus never asked you to carry.
You have been trying to be your own savior.
Every failure becomes a verdict.
Every command becomes another weight.
Every Christian who appears stronger becomes another person to compare yourself against.
Every spiritual discipline becomes another opportunity to prove yourself.
But the Gospel says:
Stop bringing God your résumé as though Christ needs your qualifications.
Bring Him your sin.
Bring Him your shame.
Bring Him the thing you keep deleting from your history but cannot erase from your memory.
Bring Him the addiction.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The lust.
The hypocrisy.
The unbelief.
The secret life.
Bring the real you to the real Jesus.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Because repentance becomes possible when you stop hiding.
The cross already tells the truth about your sin.
It was serious enough that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And the cross tells the truth about grace.
God loved sinners enough to give His Son.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”
— John 3:16
Christianity is therefore not fundamentally a self-improvement program.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ that creates a new way of living.
Paul captures the heart of it:
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
— 2 Corinthians 5:17
Not merely a more disciplined old creation.
New.
That does not mean Christians become instantly flawless.
The New Testament itself was written to churches full of people still needing correction, repentance, growth, endurance, and sanctification.
But the direction has changed.
The allegiance has changed.
The center has changed.
Jesus is no longer an accessory to life.
He becomes Lord.
And obedience becomes something astonishing:
Not payment.
Worship.
You forgive because you have been forgiven.
You pursue purity because your body belongs to Christ.
You tell the truth because you belong to the One who is truth.
You love your enemies because your King loved His enemies.
You serve because your Lord washed feet.
You resist temptation not because resisting earns salvation, but because sin is no longer your rightful master.
You open Scripture not to accumulate spiritual points, but because you want to know the God who has spoken.
You pray not to impress heaven, but because through Christ you have access to the Father.
You obey because grace has changed what obedience means.
And when you fall?
You do not call darkness light.
You confess.
You repent.
You get up.
You run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needed tonight.
You do not have to hide.
You do not need another mask.
You need Jesus.
Not because typing words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when pride finally stops protecting the image.
Not to win an argument.
Send it privately to the person who thinks their past disqualifies them forever.
Because there may come another night when failure whispers that you must earn your way back to God, and you will need to remember again:
Christ is not asking you to purchase what His blood has already secured for those who trust in Him.
Salvation cannot be bought. God’s approval cannot be purchased.
Is Christianity about following rules?
Christianity includes commands, and genuine discipleship includes obedience.
But Christianity is not salvation by rule-keeping.
At its center stands a Person.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who came for sinners.
The Savior who carried the cross.
The Lamb whose blood was shed.
The risen Lord who conquered death.
The King who calls us to repent, believe, follow, abide, obey, and become His.
Rules can tell you where you went wrong.
Only Jesus can forgive you.
Rules can expose your guilt.
Only Jesus can reconcile you to God.
Rules can describe righteous living.
Only the grace of God can save sinners and begin making them new.
So stop trying to impress the One who already knows everything.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Christ.
And then obey Him—not like a terrified prisoner attempting to earn release, but as someone whose chains have been broken and whose life now belongs to the One who set him free.
Because perhaps the greatest scandal of grace is not that God lowered His standard so sinners could enter.
He did something infinitely more costly.
Christ met the demands sinners could never satisfy, bore sin in our place, rose victorious, and now offers salvation as a gift to those who trust in Him.
Your sin does not become beautiful.
Your shame does not become your identity.
Your failure does not need to become your final sentence.
Jesus takes sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith and begins writing something grace alone could write.
So when the old voice whispers, “You failed the rules again…”
Look toward the cross.
And remember:
The Gospel was never the story of how well you could save yourself. It is the story of how completely you needed Jesus.
